issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
Elias was twenty-one, a social ministry worker newly married, when he volunteered for a three-month relief deployment in a conflict zone. His team was stationed near a village that had been shelled, distributing food and medical supplies. One afternoon, a truck backfired near the checkpoint. Elias heard shouting in Arabic-angry, urgent-and then the crack of gunfire. He dove behind a wall, his heart slamming, and for what felt like hours he lay there, certain he would die, the voices growing louder and closer before suddenly stopping. When he finally stood, the village was quiet, the shouting had ceased, and the danger was over. But the memory of that terror did not fade; it lodged itself inside him, and months later, back home in his quiet American town, the sound of a raised voice in a grocery store could send him right back behind that wall. Once the memory has surfaced, he cannot shake the sense that the danger is still present - that it has simply moved into his body rather than gone away. A raised voice in Arabic on the street drags the whole memory back - the shouting, the gunfire, the smell of dust - as if no time has passed at all. That same raised voice also triggers a feeling of immediate danger - his body tenses, his eyes scan for exits, as though the threat is already in the room with him. When he hears a raised voice in a store now, he immediately leaves the aisle, abandoning his cart, because staying would mean the memory taking hold completely.

Now, Elias cannot bear to talk about what happened. When his wife asks about his deployment, or when a coworker mentions a military family in need, the memory surges forward-not as a story he tells, but as a vivid, present terror that feels as real as the moment it happened. The memory is so extreme, so far outside anything he had ever known, that sometimes he wonders if it really happened to him at all. Yet the terror is undeniable: remembering brings back the same helplessness, the same certainty of death, and the memory feels like it is happening right now, not something that is over. These episodes leave him shaken, and he has come to believe that if he talks about the event, he will be pulled back into that moment and never fully return.

To cope, Elias has developed a careful set of routines. He avoids any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, because hope feels like a trap-a vulnerability that could be shattered. Not talking about it, not allowing himself to feel anything good, has meant the memory has never been put anywhere; it remains in him, undisturbed and intact, exactly where he left it. He stays up until very late at night, delaying sleep, because the moment he closes his eyes the memory is waiting for him, and he would rather be exhausted than relive it. The memory itself is what drives these routines - he has learned that if he keeps moving, keeps occupied, the images cannot get a foothold. When he does sleep, he wakes during the night to check that he is safe-listening for footsteps, for the wrong kind of silence. This hypervigilance has bled into his days: sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and strangers approaching him in ordinary situations feel like threats. He has come to believe that the world is filled with hidden dangers, and that he must stay watchful to survive. Already running on threat, he finds that almost anything can tip into a warning - a car door slamming, a sudden shout from a neighbor's yard - each one confirming what his body already believes. Walking home on high alert, he passes a group of men speaking loudly and the memory is simply there - pulled out of him by the adrenaline, fully formed.

The more Elias ruminate on how the event could have been prevented-if he had been faster, if he had stayed behind the wall sooner-the more the memory intrudes, sharp and terrifying, and the more threatened he feels by the ordinary world around him. Every raised voice in Arabic he hears on the street or in a store triggers the same terror, and each trigger strengthens his belief that the memory is not really over, that it could happen again at any moment. Because the memory comes back so vividly, he has begun to see threads of it everywhere - in the tone of a stranger's voice, in the sudden movement of a car, in the quality of afternoon light. His wife has noticed he no longer joins her for dinner with friends; he says he is tired, but what he cannot tell her is that he is afraid of letting his guard down, afraid that a moment of happiness will leave him defenseless.

He came to therapy because his marriage is fraying and his work is suffering. What frightens him most is the thought that this will never end-that he will always be a man hiding behind a wall, listening for the shouting to start again.

violations.explanation: No paragraph explicitly states that triggers (e.g., raised voices) cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance); they are described as co-occurring or as separate consequences.
No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to a sense of threat; the text describes them as eliciting terror and intrusions but not directly causing a feeling of danger.
No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to the trauma memory; triggers are described as bringing back terror or sending him behind the wall, but not as causing the memory itself.

No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to maladaptive strategies; the memory is described as something he avoids and that waits for him, but not as the direct cause of his routines.
No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to a sense of threat; the memory brings terror and helplessness, but not a direct feeling of danger.
No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to triggers; the memory is described as being triggered by sounds, but not as causing those triggers.
No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to the memory; threat is described as a consequence of triggers and hypervigilance, not as causing the memory.
No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to triggers; threat is described as a state that leads to hypervigilance but not as causing triggers.
No paragraph explicitly states that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to the memory; the strategies are described as coping mechanisms that prevent or delay the memory, not as causing it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph explicitly states that triggers (e.g., raised voices) cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance); they are described as co-occurring or as separate consequences.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Threat: No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to a sense of threat; the text describes them as eliciting terror and intrusions but not directly causing a feeling of danger.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: No paragraph explicitly states that triggers cause or lead to the trauma memory; triggers are described as bringing back terror or sending him behind the wall, but not as causing the memory itself.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to maladaptive strategies; the memory is described as something he avoids and that waits for him, but not as the direct cause of his routines.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to a sense of threat; the memory brings terror and helplessness, but not a direct feeling of danger.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph explicitly states that the memory causes or leads to triggers; the memory is described as being triggered by sounds, but not as causing those triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to the memory; threat is described as a consequence of triggers and hypervigilance, not as causing the memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph explicitly states that a sense of threat causes or leads to triggers; threat is described as a state that leads to hypervigilance but not as causing triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph explicitly states that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to the memory; the strategies are described as coping mechanisms that prevent or delay the memory, not as causing it.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
